title: Understanding Your Data — EDA
abstract:
Exploratory Data Analysis in four layers, following the notes exactly: asking
the basic questions (shape, head, info,
isnull().sum(), describe, duplicated, corr), then
univariate analysis, then bivariate and multivariate analysis, then automated
profiling. For each layer this document gives the plots, what each plot is
actually diagnosing, the statistics behind them (skewness, kurtosis, correlation
and its failure modes), and — most importantly — the concrete downstream
decision each finding forces.

blocks.t: The Four Layers

rows: Size, shape, dtypes, nulls, duplicates, summary statistics
One variable at a time — what does this single column look like?
Two or more together — how do they interact?

blocks.t: EDA is not decoration — every chart must change a decision

This is the discipline that separates useful EDA from a wall of plots. Before
drawing anything, ask what you would do differently depending on the
answer. A right-skewed column tells you to apply a log transform (Topic 18). Two
features correlated at 0.97 tell you one should go (Topic 43). A 60/40 class
split tells you accuracy is fine; a 99/1 split tells you it is useless
(Topic 80). If a chart changes nothing, do not make it.
Explore the training set only

Every number in this document must be computed on the training split. If you
explore the full dataset, your modelling decisions are informed by the test set
— a subtle leakage that no code review catches. Split first (Topic 10), then
explore.
Layer 1 — Asking the Basic Questions
The notes give the checklist directly, question and command:

head: Question
Command
Decides
rows: How does the data look like?
What is the data type of cols?
How does the data look mathematically?
How is the correlation between columns?

blocks.t: How to read describe()
Each row of the output answers a question:

items: count $<$ number of rows $\Rightarrow$ that column has nulls.

mean far from 50% (median) $\Rightarrow$ the column is
 skewed. Impute with the median, not the mean.

min negative on a quantity that cannot be negative (age, price,
 duration) $\Rightarrow$ a data error, not an outlier.

max enormously above 75% $\Rightarrow$ outliers or a
 sentinel value such as $9999$ or $-1$ standing in for "missing".

std differing by orders of magnitude across columns
 $\Rightarrow$ you will need feature scaling (Topics 13–14).

blocks.t: The sentinel-value trap

A column whose minimum is $-1$ or whose maximum is $999$ is often encoding
"unknown" as a number. Pandas will not flag it — isnull() returns
zero — and the model will happily learn that age $=999$ predicts something.
Always compare min and max against what is physically possible.
Layer 2 — Univariate Analysis
From the notes

One variable at a time. Basically, how does this single column look?
Check: distribution, central tendency, outliers, missing values.
Common visuals: histogram, box plot.

blocks.cap:
The univariate toolkit. Histogram shows the shape; box plot shows the
 spread and flags outliers; the ECDF answers percentile questions exactly; a
 count plot shows class balance for categoricals.

blocks.t: Distribution and skewness

blocks.cap:
The three cases. Skewness is the most actionable single number
 univariate EDA produces, because it dictates both the imputation strategy and
 the transformation.

blocks.t: Skewness and kurtosis

\text{skew} = \frac{\frac1n\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^3}{s^3},
 \qquad
 \text{kurtosis}_{\text{excess}} = \frac{\frac1n\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^4}{s^4}-3 .

Rules of thumb: $|\text{skew}|<0.5$ is roughly symmetric; $0.5$–$1$ is
moderate; $>1$ is strong. Positive excess kurtosis means heavy tails — more
extreme values than a normal distribution would produce, which is a warning that
your outlier treatment matters.

head: Finding
Meaning
Action
rows: Log / sqrt / Box-Cox (Topics 18–19); impute with median
Find the hidden grouping variable; consider two models
The column carries almost no information; consider dropping

blocks.t: Central tendency

head: Statistic
Definition
Use it when
rows: The distribution is symmetric and outlier-free
Skewed, or outliers present — it is robust

blocks.t: Spread and outliers

The box plot encodes five numbers: $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, and the whiskers at
$Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR}$ and $Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}$ where
$\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$. Anything beyond a whisker is flagged. This is exactly the
IQR outlier rule of Topic 29, and it is why the box plot is the univariate
outlier tool.
Layer 3 — Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis
From the notes

Bivariate: two variables together — how does one column change with
another? Check correlation and trends; common visual is the scatter
plot.
Multivariate: more than two variables — how do multiple columns
interact? Check combined effects and patterns; common visuals are
heatmaps and pair plots.
Choosing the plot from the dtype pair

blocks.cap: The plot is determined by the pair of data types, not by preference.

head: Pair
Plot
Statistic
rows: Box plot, violin, bar per group

blocks.t: Correlation, and the two ways it lies

blocks.cap:
Left: the correlation heatmap, with a perfectly redundant pair boxed
 in red — spend and spend_usd are the same column in different
 units. Right: a perfect deterministic relationship that Pearson correlation
 reports as approximately zero.

blocks.t: Pearson vs Spearman

r_{\text{Pearson}}=\frac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}
 {\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2}\sqrt{\sum_i (y_i-\bar y)^2}}

measures linear association only. Spearman's $\rho$ is Pearson computed
on the ranks, so it captures any monotone relationship and is
robust to outliers. If Spearman is high while Pearson is low, the relationship is
monotone but curved — a signal to apply a transform (Topic 18) rather than to
discard the feature.
The two classic correlation errors

1. $r\approx0$ does not mean "no relationship". The right-hand panel
above shows $y=x^2$ with $r\approx0$. Pearson sees only straight lines. Always
plot.

2. Correlation is not causation, and it is not multivariate. A feature
uncorrelated with the target in isolation can be highly predictive in
combination with another. Correlation-based feature selection discards such
features. Use it as a hint, not a filter.
What the heatmap is really for
Two distinct readings, and they lead to opposite actions:

items:
Feature vs target — high $|r|$ suggests a useful predictor.
 Very high $|r|$ (say $>0.95$) suggests leakage: the
 feature probably encodes the answer.

Feature vs feature — high $|r|$ signals
 multicollinearity. The model still predicts well but the
 coefficients become unstable and uninterpretable. This is the motivation
 for Ridge and Elastic Net (Topics 41, 43) and for VIF-based selection.

blocks.t: The correlation matrix misses three-way redundancy

If $x_3 = x_1 + x_2$, then $x_3$ may correlate only moderately with each of
$x_1$ and $x_2$ individually, yet it is perfectly determined by them.
Pairwise correlation cannot see this. Variance Inflation Factor can:
$\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1-R_j^2)$ where $R_j^2$ comes from regressing feature $j$ on
all the others. $\text{VIF}>10$ is the usual alarm.
Layer 4 — Pandas Profiling
From the notes

An automated EDA tool that summarises the dataset for you. Helps you
quickly understand the structure and quality of the data. Useful for
initial exploration, not final conclusions.

One call produces per-column distributions, missing-value maps, correlation
matrices, duplicate detection, and warnings for high cardinality, constant
columns and skew.

head: Good for
Not a substitute for
rows: The first ten minutes on an unfamiliar dataset
Judgement about what a finding means

blocks.t: It does not scale, and it does not think

On a wide dataset the report is enormous and slow — use minimal=True or
sample. More importantly, it reports that a column is skewed; it will
never tell you that a negative duration_seconds means your ETL is
double-subtracting timestamps. That is your job.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

pd.set_option("display.width", 120, "display.max_columns", 40)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "tenure_months": rng.integers(1, 72, n).astype(float),
    "monthly_spend": rng.lognormal(4.2, .6, n),            # right skewed
    "sessions_30d":  rng.poisson(9, n).astype(float),
    "support_calls": rng.poisson(1.1, n).astype(float),
    "plan":          rng.choice(["basic","standard","premium"], n, p=[.5,.3,.2]),
    "region":        rng.choice(["N","S","E","W"], n),
})
df["spend_usd"] = df.monthly_spend / 83                    # redundant column
df.loc[rng.random(n) < .09, "monthly_spend"] = np.nan      # realistic gaps
df.loc[rng.random(n) < .01, "tenure_months"] = 999         # sentinel trap
df["churned"] = (rng.random(n) <
                 1/(1+np.exp(-(0.35*df.support_calls - 0.05*df.tenure_months + 1)))
                ).astype(int)

# =====================================================================
# LAYER 1 -- THE BASIC QUESTIONS
# =====================================================================
print("1. how big?          ", df.shape)
print("2. how does it look? \n", df.head(3))
print("3. dtypes:");            df.info()
print("4. missing:\n",          df.isnull().sum()[lambda s: s > 0])
print("5. mathematically:\n",   df.describe().T.round(2))
print("6. duplicates:",         df.duplicated().sum())
print("7. correlation:\n",      df.corr(numeric_only=True).round(2))

# Read describe() programmatically instead of squinting at it:
d = df.describe().T
d["skew_flag"]     = (d["mean"] - d["50%"]).abs() > 0.5 * d["std"]
d["scale_needed"]  = d["std"] / d["std"].min() > 10
print(d[["mean", "50%", "std", "skew_flag", "scale_needed"]].round(2))

# THE SENTINEL TRAP: isnull() sees nothing wrong here
print("max tenure:", df.tenure_months.max())    # 999 -> physically impossible
df.loc[df.tenure_months == 999, "tenure_months"] = np.nan   # convert to a real NaN

# =====================================================================
# LAYER 2 -- UNIVARIATE
# =====================================================================
num = df.select_dtypes("number").columns.drop("churned")
cat = df.select_dtypes("object").columns

for c in num:
    s = df[c].dropna()
    print(f"{c:15s} skew {stats.skew(s):+6.2f}  kurt {stats.kurtosis(s):+6.2f}  "
          f"mean {s.mean():9.2f}  median {s.median():9.2f}")

def univariate_action(series):
    """Turn a distribution into a decision."""
    s = series.dropna()
    sk = stats.skew(s)
    if abs(sk) < 0.5:
        return "symmetric -> mean imputation, no transform"
    if sk > 1:
        return "strong RIGHT skew -> log/Box-Cox (T18-19), MEDIAN imputation"
    if sk < -1:
        return "strong LEFT skew -> square transform, MEDIAN imputation"
    return "moderate skew -> median imputation, transform optional"

for c in num:
    print(f"{c:15s} {univariate_action(df[c])}")

# class balance decides whether accuracy is even a valid metric
bal = df.churned.value_counts(normalize=True)
print("class balance:\n", bal.round(3))
print("-> accuracy is misleading; use precision/recall (T48, T80)"
      if bal.min() < .2 else "-> reasonably balanced")

# outliers, IQR rule (this is what the box plot draws)
for c in num:
    q1, q3 = df[c].quantile([.25, .75])
    iqr = q3 - q1
    mask = (df[c] < q1 - 1.5*iqr) | (df[c] > q3 + 1.5*iqr)
    if mask.sum():
        print(f"{c:15s} {mask.sum():4d} outliers "
              f"outside [{q1-1.5*iqr:.1f}, {q3+1.5*iqr:.1f}]")

# =====================================================================
# LAYER 3 -- BIVARIATE / MULTIVARIATE
# =====================================================================
# numeric vs numeric: Pearson AND Spearman -- the gap is the message
for c in num:
    s = df[[c, "churned"]].dropna()
    p = stats.pearsonr(s[c], s.churned)[0]
    r = stats.spearmanr(s[c], s.churned)[0]
    flag = "  <- monotone but NON-LINEAR: transform it" if abs(r) - abs(p) > .1 else ""
    print(f"{c:15s} pearson {p:+.3f}  spearman {r:+.3f}{flag}")

# categorical vs categorical: crosstab + chi-square + Cramer's V
ct = pd.crosstab(df.plan, df.churned)
chi2, pval, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (len(df) * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))
print(ct, f"\nchi2 p={pval:.2e}  Cramer's V={cramers_v:.3f}")

# categorical vs numeric: group statistics
print(df.groupby("plan")[["monthly_spend", "sessions_30d"]].agg(["mean", "median"]).round(1))

# MULTICOLLINEARITY: pairwise
corr = df[num].corr().abs()
upper = corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
redundant = [(i, j, round(upper.loc[i, j], 3))
             for i in upper.index for j in upper.columns
             if pd.notna(upper.loc[i, j]) and upper.loc[i, j] > .95]
print("redundant pairs:", redundant)   # finds monthly_spend / spend_usd

# MULTICOLLINEARITY: VIF catches what pairwise correlation cannot
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
def vif(frame):
    X = frame.dropna()
    out = {}
    for c in X.columns:
        r2 = LinearRegression().fit(X.drop(columns=c), X[c]).score(
                 X.drop(columns=c), X[c])
        out[c] = np.inf if r2 >= 1 else 1 / (1 - r2)
    return pd.Series(out).sort_values(ascending=False)
print("VIF (>10 is a problem):\n", vif(df[num]).round(2))

# LEAKAGE CHECK: a feature that correlates ~1.0 with the target is the target
leaky = [c for c in num
         if abs(df[[c,"churned"]].dropna().corr().iloc[0,1]) > .95]
print("suspected leakage:", leaky)

# =====================================================================
# LAYER 4 -- AUTOMATED PROFILING
# =====================================================================
# pip install ydata-profiling      (formerly pandas-profiling)
# from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport
# ProfileReport(df, title="EDA", minimal=True).to_file("eda.html")
#
# minimal=True skips the expensive pairwise interactions -- essential on
# wide data. Treat the output as a starting point, never as a conclusion.

# =====================================================================
# THE PLOTS
# =====================================================================
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13, 7))
df.monthly_spend.hist(bins=40, ax=ax[0,0]);          ax[0,0].set_title("histogram")
df.boxplot(column="monthly_spend", ax=ax[0,1]);      ax[0,1].set_title("box plot")
df.plan.value_counts().plot.bar(ax=ax[0,2]);         ax[0,2].set_title("count plot")
ax[1,0].scatter(df.tenure_months, df.monthly_spend, s=4, alpha=.4)
ax[1,0].set_title("scatter (bivariate)")
df.boxplot(column="monthly_spend", by="plan", ax=ax[1,1])
im = ax[1,2].imshow(df[num].corr(), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax[1,2].set_title("correlation heatmap"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1,2])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("eda.png", dpi=140)
Worked Examples
Univariate EDA on one column
Column salary_lakh for 7 students: $x = [12,\,15,\,15,\,18,\,20,\,22,\,95]$.
Step 1 – central tendency.
The mean (28.14) is pulled up by the value 95; the median (18) is not. A large gap between mean and median is the first sign of skew or an outlier.
Step 2 – spread. Sample standard deviation $s \approx 29.67$. The IQR is computed from the quartiles $Q_1 = 15$ and $Q_3 = 21$:
Step 3 – outlier check. Fence $= Q_3 + 1.5\cdot\text{IQR} = 21 + 9 = 30$. The value $95 > 30$, so it is flagged as an outlier.

Interpretation. The univariate picture says: right-skewed, one extreme point, and a median that describes the typical student far better than the mean. This is exactly what the histogram and box plot would show, and it motivates a transformation or outlier treatment later in the pipeline.
Bivariate EDA: correlation
Two columns over 5 rows: $a = [1,2,3,4,5]$ and $b = [2,4,5,4,5]$.
Step 1 – deviations. $\bar a = 3$, $\bar b = 4$.
Step 2 – covariance numerator and variances.
\sum (a-\bar a)^2 = 10, \qquad \sum (b-\bar b)^2 = 6
Step 3 – Pearson $r$.
r = \frac{6}{\sqrt{10 \cdot 6}} = \frac{6}{7.746} \approx 0.775
Reading it. $r \approx 0.77$ is a strong positive linear relationship. A scatter plot is still required before trusting it: $r$ measures only linear association and is sensitive to a single outlier.
Summary
Everything on one page

 Visuals: histogram, box plot. Skewness is the most actionable
 output — it decides both the transform and the imputation statistic.

Layer 3 — bivariate: two columns. Check correlation and

Pearson measures linear association only; Spearman captures any
 monotone relationship. A gap between them means "transform this
 feature".

Feature–target correlation $>0.95$ means leakage. Feature–feature
 correlation $>0.95$ means multicollinearity. VIF catches

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. A feature has correlation 0.02 with the target. Drop it?

No. Pearson measures linear association only, and correlation is pairwise. The
feature may have a strong non-linear relationship (check Spearman and plot it),
or may be predictive only in interaction with another feature. Use a model-based
importance measure before dropping anything.
Q. Mean 45{,}000, median 32{,}000. What does that tell you?

Strong right skew — a long tail of high earners. Consequences: impute with the
median, not the mean; consider a log transform before any distance- or
gradient-based model; and expect the IQR outlier rule to flag the upper tail
heavily.
Q. Two features correlate at 0.98. What do you do, and does it matter?

It depends on the model. For linear or logistic regression it matters a great
deal — coefficients become unstable and uninterpretable, so drop one, combine
them, or use Ridge. For tree ensembles, predictive performance is largely
unaffected, but the feature importance is split arbitrarily between the two.
Q. Why explore only the training set?

Because decisions made from EDA — which transform, which imputation, which
features — are part of modelling. Making them with knowledge of the test set
contaminates it, and the resulting test score is optimistic.
Q. When is a box plot better than a histogram?

For comparing several groups side by side, and for outlier detection, since it
draws the IQR rule directly. The histogram is better for seeing the actual shape
— a box plot cannot show bimodality, which is exactly the finding that would
tell you two populations are mixed in one column.
